chapter.title: Plan the route

cards.body: Why do you remember three things from a good talk and nothing from a bad one? Because the good speaker told you where you were going, took you there in three steps, and told you when you'd arrived. **A route has a start, a few landmarks and an end**; a bad talk is a wander with no map.

cards.prompt: Priya has 3 minutes to tell her running club why they should switch to morning runs. Which opening puts her listeners on the route?

options.text: "So, I've been thinking a lot about running lately, and there are so many factors..."
"Morning runs will get more of us to turn up. Here's why, in three steps."
"Let me start with how our club began, and who was there..."

whyNot.a: That's the wander, not the route: nobody knows where they're being taken.
whyNot.c: That's starting the walk at the wrong end: how the club began might be a step, but it isn't the destination.

cards.reteach: The first line of a talk is a signpost. It names the destination so listeners can relax and follow. Anything that delays the signpost is the speaker wandering while everyone waits.

cards.title: Signpost, then three landmarks
cards.body:
A 3-minute talk has three parts, and the first is a *signpost*: one sentence that says where you're all heading. That's your sentence from chapter 1. Say it in the first 20 seconds and your listeners stop guessing.

Then the middle: **three steps, no more**. Three is small enough to hold in a head without notes, and big enough to feel like a journey. Think of walking a friend to the bakery: past the church, over the bridge, left at the red door.

Each step gets about 40 seconds. One idea, one example, then you move.

cards.title: Tomas and the coffee machine
cards.body: Tomas has 3 minutes to get his 3 flatmates to buy a shared coffee machine, and his signpost is 'A shared machine saves us money and the morning queue.' Step 1: the four of them spend about 12 pounds a day at the café, which he counted for a week. Step 2: a decent machine costs 180 pounds, so it pays for itself in about 15 days. Step 3: nobody has to stand behind the man who orders 6 oat flat whites. He **closes with the signpost sentence again**, word for word, and sits down.

cards.prompt: Lena is planning a 3-minute talk for her book club: 'We should meet every 2 weeks, not monthly.' She has 5 reasons on a sticky note. What does she do with them?

options.text: Say all 5 quickly, about 30 seconds each, so nothing is lost.
Pick the 3 strongest, give each about 40 seconds, and drop the other 2.
Keep all 5 but merge them into one long middle section with no steps.

whyNot.a: That's a sprint, not a walk: 5 steps in 3 minutes leaves no room for an example on any of them.
whyNot.c: That's the wander: one long middle gives listeners no landmarks to hold onto.

cards.reteach: Three steps is a limit, not a target you round up from. If you have 5 reasons, 2 of them are weaker. Cut those and give the remaining 3 room to breathe, about 40 seconds each.

cards.title: Arrive, and say so
cards.body:
The third part is the shortest and the most skipped: **say where you've arrived**. Repeat your signpost sentence, nearly word for word. You'd think repeating yourself sounds lazy. To a listener it sounds like landing.

Now put the whole route on one index card. Line 1: the signpost. Lines 2 to 4: your three steps, each as 3 or 4 words, like 'café costs: 12 a day'. Line 5: the signpost again.

That card is your map. If you can read it in 10 seconds, you can walk the talk in 3 minutes.

Dev wrote his route the night before: signpost, three steps, close. Then mid-walk he thought of a fourth point and a 'quick story', so 3 steps became 6 and his close became 'anyway, yeah, that's about it'. You can spot this from the room: the speaker glances at the clock, and the listeners glance at each other. **A fourth step is a detour**, not a bonus.

cards.prompt: A friend shows you their index card for tomorrow's talk: one opening line, 3 short steps, and nothing else. What's missing?

options.text: Nothing. The close is optional for a short talk.
A closing line that repeats the opening sentence.
Two more steps, so the talk feels thorough.

whyNot.a: That's Dev's mistake from the other side: with no close, you trail off instead of landing.
whyNot.c: That's the detour: 5 steps in 3 minutes rushes every one of them.

cards.reteach: A route has three parts, not two. Signpost, three steps, then the signpost again so everyone knows the walk has ended. The close is one line, and it's the line people carry home.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body:
A 3-minute talk is a walk with **three parts**: say where you're going, go there in 3 steps of about 40 seconds each, then say you've arrived by repeating your first sentence. The whole route fits on one index card you can read in 10 seconds.

Tomorrow: the only line worth memorising word for word, and why it isn't the close.
Take your chapter 1 sentence. On an index card or a phone note, write it as **line 1 and line 5**. Fill lines 2 to 4 with three steps, 4 words each. Read the card aloud once.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now lay out a 3-minute talk on one index card: an opening line, 3 steps and a closing line that repeats the opening.
